source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: On five non-reasoning models, a 'think step by step' prompt raised average GPQA Diamond accuracy against an 'answer directly' prompt, but made some previously-easy questions fail.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, 25 trials each (4,950 runs per cell). Average rating gain vs Direct: Gemini Flash 2.0 +13.5 points, Sonnet 3.5 +11.7 (both p<.001), GPT-4o-mini +4.4 (p=.067, ns). 100%-correct metric: Sonnet 3.5 +10.1, GPT-4o +1.0 (ns), Gemini Flash 2.0 -13.1, Gemini Pro 1.5 -17.2 (p<.001). CoT took 35-600% longer.
limits: One benchmark, simple CoT wording, temperature 0, 2024-2025 models. The 'Direct' arm told the model not to think, which is itself a handicap.
agent_relevance: The CoT gain is partly an artefact of forbidding reasoning in the baseline. Measure our scaffold against the model's default, not against a muzzled baseline (G7).

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: Compared with the default prompt, explicit CoT gave little or nothing on non-reasoning models, and only marginal gains on reasoning models.
numbers: Default vs CoT, average rating: Gemini Flash 2.0 +6.2 (p<.001), GPT-4o +6.9 (p=.003), Sonnet 3.5 -1.9 (ns), GPT-4o-mini +0.4 (ns). Reasoning models vs Direct: o3-mini +2.9 (p=.024), o4-mini +3.1 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -3.3 (p=.005); Flash 2.5 also -13.1 on the 100%-correct metric. CoT cost 20-80% more time on reasoning models.
quote: For dedicated reasoning models, the added benefits of explicit CoT prompting appear negligible
limits: Only GPQA Diamond and three reasoning models. Authors say tailored CoT prompts might do more.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 in part: for current reasoning models a generic stepwise instruction adds about 3 points or less and costs tokens. A scaffold that only restates 'think step by step' should not be expected to help.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: Many recent models already write a short reasoning trace when given no instruction. Telling them to answer with no explanation hurts them.
numbers: Table S1 documents default CoT-like output. Default prompt vs CoT: no significant change on the 51%-correct metric for any non-reasoning model. Different CoT wordings had negligible effect (Figure S3).
agent_relevance: Our baseline arm must be the model's default behaviour, and token cost must be reported next to accuracy.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) If Multi-Agent Debate is the Answer, What is the Question? (Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate)
finding: Five debate frameworks (SoM, Multi-Persona, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse) rarely beat plain CoT and lose to self-consistency, across 9 benchmarks and 4 models, at matched number of LLM calls (6).
numbers: GPT-4o-mini: MMLU CoT 80.73, SC 82.13, SoM 74.73; GSM8K CoT 93.60, SC 95.67, SoM 94.93; MATH CoT 72.87, SC 73.96, SoM 75.40; MMLU-Pro CoT 62.80, SC 66.27. Over 36 configurations (4 models x 9 datasets), SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT significantly in only about 15% of cases; Multi-Persona never. Debate did beat the single direct answer in 34 of 45 GPT-4o-mini conditions.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
limits: Models: GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b, Claude-3.5-haiku. Not reasoning models. Temperature 1. SC excluded on code tasks. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 4 for non-reasoning models: debate is not worth its cost against voting. Debate on math did relatively better (SoM GSM8K and MATH above CoT). G9 stands.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) If Multi-Agent Debate is the Answer, What is the Question? (Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate)
finding: Token-matched scaling: self-consistency improves as budget grows, debate does not scale cleanly.
numbers: Figure 6 and text: SC 'effectively utilizes the increased inference budget'; SoM does not stably improve on MMLU with more tokens; EoT improves on MMLU and GSM8K with more tokens but stays below SC. More agents (3 to 9) or rounds (2 to 4) mostly gave stagnation or decline.
limits: Exact values only in figures (not read numerically).
agent_relevance: Spend extra compute on independent samples with a vote, not on longer argument, unless an outside check exists.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) If Multi-Agent Debate is the Answer, What is the Question? (Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate)
finding: Debate methods both fix wrong answers and break right ones. Aggressive ones (Multi-Persona, ChatEval, AgentVerse) change many correct answers; conservative ones (SoM, EoT) change few.
numbers: Figure 4 compares corrected vs newly wrong answers against a direct single agent on each dataset; counts are in the figure, text gives the pattern only.
agent_relevance: Same failure as intrinsic self-correction (Huang 2024): a critic with no outside signal can overturn a correct answer. Gate revisions on a verifier (G9).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) If Multi-Agent Debate is the Answer, What is the Question? (Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate)
finding: Mixing different base models inside debate (Heter-MAD) improved results where same-model debate did not.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini + Llama3.1-70b: SoM-Heter average over 9 datasets 76.7 vs SoM-GPT 74.3, SoM-Llama 69.9, CoT-Average 72.5. SoM-Heter MMLU 83.5, MMLU-Pro 65.0, AGIEval 70.1, GSM8K 94.6, HumanEval 75.8.
limits: Two-model pool only; the authors did not optimise the design. Relevant to epistemic diversity, not to a single-model agent.
agent_relevance: One agent cannot copy this. Diversity must come from different roles or independent samples, with the caveat that same-model personas gave only small gains (Du 2023 persona result).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Storing every past run (add-all) made agents worse than a fixed small memory; storing only runs judged correct by a strict (oracle) evaluator made them best. Coarse LLM judges were in between and often no better than the fixed memory.
numbers: Success rate/accuracy (RegAgent, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT): Fixed 67.53/16.75/40.11/71.50; Add-all 55.48/13.05/32.32/59.90; Coarse C1 63.18/26.19/36.92/74.00; C2 65.78/32.21/40.01/68.80; C3 (judge fine-tuned on 300 correct labels) 67.35/34.66/47.37/79.50; Strict 70.95/38.50/51.00/85.40. Memory sizes: add-all 4100/2411/2125/1050 records vs strict 2938/1012/1178/904.
quote: noisy or low-quality additions can harm memory utility
limits: Strict evaluator is a ground-truth oracle (simulated human). Four agent systems, mostly 2024-2025 GPT-4o-class models. Not token-matched against a no-memory run.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5: gating lesson storage on verified success matters. An ungated lesson store can fall below a small static one. Store lessons only after an external check (G9, S9).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy the outputs of retrieved memories when the new task looks similar (experience-following). So an error in a stored record spreads to later tasks, and correct-looking records can still mislead.
numbers: Output similarity tracks input similarity with Pearson r close to 1 under add-all. Using error-free stored outputs beats using agent outputs; add-all and coarse selection widen the gap over time. With strict addition AgentDriver lags at first, then passes the error-free baseline after about 2000 executions. Future task outcomes can be used as free quality labels for deletion.
limits: Deletion numbers not extracted. Similarity measured with embedding-based scores.
agent_relevance: Direct design rule for the lesson store: tag each lesson with its verified outcome, drop lessons whose later uses fail, and avoid verbatim retrieval of near-duplicate past answers.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion's gain depends on the signal that triggers reflection. Without unit tests the agent made harmful edits; without the written self-reflection step the loop did no better than baseline.
numbers: HumanEval Rust, 50 hardest problems, GPT-4: base 0.60; no test generation (self-reflection only) 0.52; tests but no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68. HotPotQA, 100 questions: adding the self-reflection step gave about 8 points more than episodic memory of the last trajectory alone.
limits: Small subsets (50 and 100 items). Authors' own system. GPT-4 on 2023 benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Confirms the gating principle: reflection with a real test beats reflection alone; reflection without a test hurts (G9).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval Python (base GPT-4 80%), but lost on MBPP Python because self-written tests passed wrong code.
numbers: Table 1: HumanEval PY 0.80 to 0.91; MBPP PY 0.80 to 0.77; HumanEval Rust 0.60 to 0.68; MBPP Rust 0.71 to 0.75. False-positive rate (tests pass, code wrong): MBPP Python 16.3%, HumanEval Python 1.4%.
limits: No external held-out verifier; the MBPP failure comes from the model grading itself. No ablation that gates memory writes.
agent_relevance: Gate quality equals gain. When the self-made check is flaky, the loop can stop early on a wrong answer.

source: Wang et al. (2025) From Harm to Help: Turning Reasoning In-Context Demos into Assets for Reasoning LMs
finding: Worked solutions placed in context lower accuracy of reasoning models, even high-quality retrieved R1 traces. More demos hurt more. This is an LLM version of the expertise reversal effect.
numbers: Qwen3 (1.5B, 3B, 8B) and R1-Distill (7B, 32B) vs direct zero-shot. AIME'25: 1-shot drop about 6-16 points, 3-shot drop up to 35 points. GPQA Diamond: 1-shot drop 1-5, 3-shot drop 4-8. Demos retrieved from OpenThoughts-114k by question similarity. Two mechanisms: semantic misguidance (model copies steps verbatim) and strategy transfer failure.
limits: Open models, two benchmarks, retrieved demos. Not a test of human-style expertise reversal; the cause is copying, not redundancy.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 in part. For a strong thinker, do not paste full worked solutions of similar problems into the prompt. Give short abstracted insights instead.

source: Wang et al. (2025) From Harm to Help: Turning Reasoning In-Context Demos into Assets for Reasoning LMs
finding: Turning demos into abstract insights, then solving the target alone (Insight-to-Solve) beat direct answering, so the harm is in how examples are used, not in examples as such.
numbers: Table 1 (Direct / I2S / I2S+): R1-Distill-Qwen-7B AIME25 42.00 / 48.00 / 51.33, GPQA 51.26 / 53.30 / 55.16; R1-Distill-Qwen-14B AIME25 50.00 / 54.00 / 60.00, GPQA 59.50 / 59.60 / 63.03; Qwen3-1.7B AIME25 35.96 / 41.32 / 42.65. Abstract: GPT-4.1 +14.0 on AIME'25, o1-mini +2.7 AIME and +1.7 GPQA. Self-Refine and Progressive-Hint baselines gained less.
limits: Authors' own method, small models in the main table, extra calls cost tokens (not token-matched).
agent_relevance: Supports the schema choice of lessons as abstract rules rather than solved cases.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: The developers advise zero-shot prompting for their reasoning model because few-shot prompting consistently lowers its accuracy.
numbers: No number given in the text. Appendix: MMLU-Pro, C-Eval and CLUE-WSC original few-shot prompts were changed to zero-shot because 'the CoT in few-shot may hurt the performance of DeepSeek-R1'.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: Statement of practice, no ablation table. One model family.
agent_relevance: Same direction as d12; reasoning-trained models gain from a plain problem statement and a format spec.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? Journal of Educational Psychology 103(1)
finding: Unassisted discovery is worse than explicit instruction; enhanced (guided) discovery is better than other methods. 164 studies in two meta-analyses.
numbers: Unassisted vs explicit: 580 comparisons from 108 studies, d = -0.38 (CI -0.44 to -0.31 in the abstract; -0.50 to -0.25 at study level), Q(107)=522.11. Enhanced vs other: 360 comparisons from 56 studies, d = +0.30 (CI .23 to .36). First-tier journals d=-0.67 vs second tier -0.24; unpublished -0.01. Dropping the 24 physical-skill comparisons moved enhanced from 0.30 to 0.25.
quote: The findings suggest that unassisted discovery does not benefit learners, whereas feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, and elicited explanations do.
limits: Heterogeneous comparison conditions. Effects depend on domain: math -0.16, science -0.39, problem solving -0.48, verbal/social -0.95.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 7. Giving no guidance and expecting the agent to find the method alone is the weak arm; guided steps are the strong arm.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? Journal of Educational Psychology 103(1)
finding: Inside the explicit arm, worked examples and feedback beat unassisted discovery most. In the enhanced arm, elicited explanation and guided discovery help, but 'generation' tasks do not.
numbers: Unassisted discovery vs: worked examples d=-0.63, feedback -0.46, direct teaching -0.29, explanations provided -0.28. Enhanced types: guided discovery d=0.50, elicited explanation 0.36, generation -0.15. Enhanced vs worked examples d=0.06 (ns). Adults gained more from enhanced discovery than children; reaction time and mental-load measures went the other way.
limits: Study-level coding choices; four of five unpublished studies used generation tasks.
agent_relevance: Worked examples are not beaten by guided discovery (0.06, ns). Combine a worked case, an explanation request, and feedback from an outside check.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS 122
finding: In a field RCT of nearly 1,000 high-school students, plain GPT-4 help raised practice scores but lowered later unaided exam scores. A tutor prompt with hints and teacher-written solutions removed the harm.
numbers: Practice grades +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor). Unaided exam: GPT Base -17% vs control (significant); GPT Tutor effect 'essentially eradicated', no positive effect. Four 90-minute sessions, about fifty classes in grades 9-11. Students often copied solutions from GPT Base; they did not perceive any drop in their learning.
quote: students in the GPT Base arm perform statistically significantly worse than students in the control arm by 17%
limits: One school, one subject, one model (GPT-4). Exam problems closely mirrored practice problems. The PNAS erratum (Aug 2025) only fixes an author affiliation. No independent replication found in this search.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 8 (numbers now read from the paper). Agent analogue not found: Xiong d09 is the nearest (stored outputs get copied later).

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design. Scientific Reports
finding: The paper does not ablate its tutor design. The tutor combined a system prompt (active engagement, cognitive load, growth mindset), a platform that moves students through multi-part problems in sequence, and prompts holding step-by-step expert solutions.
numbers: Median post-score 4.5 (N=142 lesson-level observations) vs 3.5 (N=174) in class; pre-test baseline 2.75 (N=316); rank-sum z=-5.6; median time on task 49 minutes vs about 60 in class; 83% rated explanations as good as or better than the instructor's.
limits: Crossover, one physics course at one university, first-exposure material at understand/apply/analyse level. Authors say results may not hold for complex synthesis and higher-order critical thinking. No element tested alone, so gap 3 stays open.
agent_relevance: Which part drives the gain is unknown. The authors credit step-by-step solutions in the prompt for accuracy, consistent with Sprague 2025 (CoT helps maths).

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design. Scientific Reports
finding: The authors report that a system prompt alone could not keep the tutor on sequence across multi-part problems; the platform had to enforce order.
numbers: Text: the AI tutor 'would occasionally discuss parts out of sequence or that were not immediately relevant', so the platform guided students sequentially. Self-pacing was seen in the time distribution (70% under 60 minutes, 30% over).
limits: Design note, no measurement of how often it happened.
agent_relevance: For our agent: ordering of steps (states S0-S9) should be enforced by the harness, not left to a prompt instruction.
